newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's single market works, but could do better.
newsitem.headline: EU's single market works, but could do better.

text.p: The European Union's single market has helped create between 300,000 and 900,000 jobs, increased the EU's income and lowered inflation, the European Commission said on Wednesday.

But the 15-nation bloc's executive, in unveiling the results of 38 economic impact studies of the exercise, said EU countries were still not doing enough to tap the single market's full potential to create jobs, growth and competitiveness.
"Now, we can see that rather by working by faith, we can work by sight. We can see concrete results," Mario Monti, the European Commissioner responsible for the market told a news conference.
"We can still do better. There are gaps to be plugged," he said, saying the expected start of a single European currency on January 1, 1999 would make the market more efficient.

According to the Commission's first figures on the impact on goods, services, capital and people of the single market, which took effect on January 1, 1993, EU gross domestic product was 1.1- to 1.5-percent higher in 1994 than it would have been.
It also said inflation rates were 1.0- to 1.5-percent lower than they would have been if the market had never happened.
In addition, it said the single market helped attract foreign directive investment to the EU.

But the Commission said "delays in applying and enforcing single market rules at (a) national level continue to limit the single market's positive contribution to growth, (competitition) and more employment."
Monti said the EU had made little progress on abolishing passport checks on people, harmonising taxation and creating EU rules on company law.
He said just over half of the legislation necessary to make the market work was fully applied in all member states, although the figure would be 85 percent if Greece's record was omitted.

He also said he favoured powers to penalise EU member states for breaches of single market rules, and the Commission was working to simplify the legislation where possible and has vowed to crack down on EU member states that do not enforce the rules.
Among the single market's successes, the Commission said the abolition of customs red tape had saved intra-EU traders Ecu five billion ($6 billion) a year.

Although EU member states had a poor record when it came to applying legislation intended to open EU public markets, public purchases of non-domestic origin increased from six percent in 1987 to 10 percent of total public sector purchases in 1994.

In the car industry, the Commission said, the move from separate national systems to a single EU system for type approval had led to savings of up to Ecus 30 million ($36 million) for car manufacturers through a 10-percent reduction in the cost of developing a new model.

It said telecommunications equipment prices have dropped by around seven percent between 1985 to 1995 due to single market measures, resulting in annual cost savings of between Ecus 1.5 billion ($1.8 billion) and two billion Ecus ($2.4 billion).

It also noted the number of cross-border branches in the banking sector had increased between 1993 and 1995 and that the price of phone calls to the United States had dropped by some 42 percent between 1990 and 1995.
